rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taste originally refers to the mouth, then metaphorically means to undergo a trial or test something.
rows.anchor: ثم قد يستعار فيوضع موضع الابتلاء والاختبار، تقول في الكلام:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shammakh uses tasted for testing a bow by drawing it to learn whether it is pliant or hard.
rows.anchor: فذاق فأعطته من اللين جانبا ... كفى ولها أن تعرق السهم حاجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses tasted for God testing the minds of Qays; finding them weak, He rejected them.
rows.anchor: وإن الله ذاق حلوم قيس ... فلما راء خفتها قلاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns Meccans, formerly secure and settled, whom God replaced with fear of the Prophet's raids and seven years of famine, until they ate hides and bones.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية نزلت في أهل مكة، وكانوا آمنين بها لا يغار عليهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garment of hunger and fear is their visible effect: emaciation, pallor, bodily exhaustion, changed circumstances, and gloom.
rows.anchor: ولباس الجوع والخوف: ما ظهر عليهم من سوء آثارهما بالضمر والشحوب ونهكة البدن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garment of piety means its outward signs: tranquility, humility, and good works; garment can denote a condition's visible effect.
rows.anchor: أي ما ظهر عنه من السكينة والإخبات والعمل الصالح، وكما تقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who are with their Lord are the angels.
rows.anchor: يعني الملائكة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ones sent in succession are angels, following one another with what God commands them to deliver.
rows.anchor: والمرسلات عرفا (1) [المرسلات: 1] يعني الملائكة، يريد: أنها متتابعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root image is a horse's mane, whose hairs form an even line; the word extends to people following one another in a group.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا من عرف الفرس، لأنه سطر مستو بعضه في إثر بعض.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression sending something with al-ʿurf means sending it with goodness or what is recognized as good.
rows.anchor: ويقال: أرسلت بالعرف أي بالمعروف.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istidrāj is to bring people gradually toward punishment without their awareness, sudden attack, or open confrontation.
rows.anchor: والاستدراج: أن يدنيهم من بأسه قليلا قليلا من حيث لا يعلمون، ولا يباغتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab usage also applies istidrāj to drawing information out gradually instead of confronting someone directly with questions.
rows.anchor: ومنه يقال: درجت فلانا إلى كذا وكذا، واستدرج فلانا حتى تعرف ما عنده وما صنع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal translation of striking their ears would be unintelligible; translating it as putting them to sleep conveys the meaning rather than the wording.
rows.anchor: إن أردت أن تنقله بلفظه، لم يفهمه المنقول إليه، فإن قلت: أنمناهم سنين عددا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about not falling deaf and blind on God's signs likewise needs a meaning-based rendering such as they did not feign inattention.
rows.anchor: إن ترجمته بمثل لفظه استغلق، وإن قلت: لم يتغافلوا أديت المعنى بلفظ آخر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says later critics accused the Qur'an of contradiction, impossibility, faulty grammar, and disordered style, although its eloquent opponents had challenged it only as magic, soothsaying, or ancient tales.
rows.anchor: وقد اعترض كتاب الله بالطعن ملحدون ولغوا فيه وهجروا، واتبعوا ما تشابه منه ابتغاء الفتنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says he compiled explanations from tafsir, expanded them, and drew on Arab language to show metaphor and possible readings without imposing an unsupported personal interpretation.
rows.anchor: فألفت هذا الكتاب، جامعا لتأويل مشكل القرآن، مستنبطا ذلك من التفسير بزيادة في الشرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is answering people who thought He would neither resurrect the dead nor gather their decayed bones.
rows.anchor: هذا رد من الله عليهم، وذلك أنهم ظنوا أن الله لا ينشر الموتى، ولا يقدر على جمع العظام البالية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can restore even the tiny finger joints and assemble them precisely; whoever can do that can more easily gather the larger bones.
rows.anchor: فقال: بلى، فاعلموا أنا نقدر على رد السلاميات على صغرها، ونؤلف بينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates the proof with a challenge about threading a bitter gourd, answered by an even finer comparison involving mustard.
rows.anchor: مثل هذا رجل قلت له: أتراك تقدر على أن تؤلف هذا الحنظل في خيط؟ فيقول لك: نعم وبين الخردل.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explains the phrase as a person repeatedly saying, 'I will repent later.'
rows.anchor: فقال سعيد بن جبير يقول: سوف أتوب، سوف أتوب.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the person commits many sins and postpones repentance.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: يكثر الذنوب، ويؤخر التوبة.

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other interpreters say the person wishes to commit sin.
rows.anchor: ويؤخر التوبة. وقال آخرون: يتمنى الخطيئة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible reading, if intended by God, takes fujūr as denying Resurrection: whoever denies the truth has deviated from it.
rows.anchor: وفيه قول آخر: على طريق الإمكان- إن كان الله تعالى أراده- وهو: أن يكون الفجور بمعنى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root sense of fujūr is deviation; a liar, denier, or sinner is called fājir because he departs from the truth.
rows.anchor: وأصل الفجور: الميل، فقيل للكاذب والمكذب والفاسق: فاجر لأنه مال عن الحق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Bedouin poem uses fajara to mean 'lied,' asking God to forgive ʿUmar if he lied about the camels.
rows.anchor: فاغفر له اللهم إن كان فجر أي: كذب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba prefers 'deny the Resurrection before him': it fits between the question about gathering bones and the question of when Resurrection will occur.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه حسن لأن الفجور اعتراض بين كلامين من أسباب يوم القيامة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba glosses the command in the spoils passage as distributing them evenly among yourselves and then obeying God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: يشاء فاتقوا الله وأصلحوا ذات بينكم. أي فرقوها بينكم على السواء وأطيعوا الله ورسوله فيما بعد إن كنتم مؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison means the believers' resentment over the spoils resembled their reluctance to set out with the Prophet; an implied phrase connects the two complaints.
rows.anchor: كأنه قال: هذا من كراهيتهم كما أخرجك وإياهم ربك وهم كارهون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anonymous poet omits 'leave me' after 'but'; the sense is to leave his body for the hyena called Umm ʿĀmir to eat.
rows.anchor: فلا تدفنوني إن دفني محرم ... عليكم، ولكن خامري أم عامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAntarah's curse implies a prayer that the she-camel's udder be denied milk, so she neither conceives nor nurses.
rows.anchor: هل تبلغني دارها شدنية ... لعنت بمحروم الشراب مصرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poet's curse means the camel should fail to conceive or, if pregnant, miscarry before term.
rows.anchor: ملعونة بعقر أو خادج أي: دعي عليها أن لا تحمل، وإن حملت: أن تلقي ولدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proverb 'Perhaps Ghuwayr brings misfortune' predicts harm coming from Ghuwayr, a water place also said to mean a diminutive of cave.
rows.anchor: ومن أمثال العرب: (عسى الغوير أبؤسا) أي: أن يأتينا من قبل الغوير بأس ومكروه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted sense is that worldly provision is shared, while in the afterlife it is exclusive to believers.
rows.anchor: أي هي للذين آمنوا- يعني في الدنيا- مشتركة، وفي الآخرة خالصة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object is 'you': Satan frightens you by means of his allies.
rows.anchor: أي يخوفكم بأوليائه، كما قال سبحانه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied object is the people: the messenger warns them of a severe punishment from God.
rows.anchor: كما قال سبحانه: لينذر بأسا شديدا من لدنه [الكهف: 2] أي لينذركم ببأس شديد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means there is no turning away from the caller for them.
rows.anchor: وقوله: يومئذ يتبعون الداعي لا عوج له [طه: 108] أي لا عوج لهم عنه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sense is that one should know to whom all honor belongs.
rows.anchor: أي يعلم أن العزة لمن هي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted sense is that God does not want them to provide for themselves.
rows.anchor: ما أريد منهم من رزق [الذاريات: 57] أي ما أريد أن يرزقوا أنفسهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object is any of God's creatures: He does not want them to feed anyone.
rows.anchor: وما أريد أن يطعمون [الذاريات: 57] أي ما أريد أن يطعموا أحدا من خلقي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat does not mean literally cutting the Prophet's aorta; it means killing him, as though his aorta had been cut.
rows.anchor: ولم يرد أنا نقطعه بعينه، فيما يرى أهل النظر، ولكنه أراد: ولو كذب علينا لأمتناه أو قتلناه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said the poisoned morsel from Khaybar continued to trouble him, and that this was the time it had cut his aorta.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ما زالت أكلة خيبر تعادني، فهذا أوان قطعت أبهري»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abhar is a vein connected to the heart; if severed, its owner dies.
rows.anchor: والأبهر: عرق يتصل بالقلب إذا انقطع مات صاحبه.

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the branding on the snout literally as God marking the person's face black on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: ذهب بعض المفسرين فيه: إلى أن الله عز وجل يسم وجهه يوم القيامة بالسواد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba prefers the Arab metaphor: branding someone with a bad mark means attaching an enduring disgrace, like an indelible brand.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب للرجل يسب الرجل سبة قبيحة، أو ينثو عليه فاحشة: وقد وسمه بميسم سوء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarīr says he branded al-Farazdaq and cut al-Akhtal's nose through satire, leaving them lasting disgrace.
rows.anchor: لما وضعت الفرزدق ميسمي ... وعلى البعيث، جدعت أنف الأخطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarīr says his satire of Mujāshiʿ and al-Zinbarī travelled on camels and was sung across land and sea.
rows.anchor: رفع المطي بما وسمت مجاشعا ... والزنبري يعوم ذو الإجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarīr compares his poetry to a fire and his satire to branding irons.
rows.anchor: وأوقدت ناري بالحديد فأصبحت ... لها وهج يصلي به الله من يصلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kumayt describes his poem as branding groups; al-ʿilāṭ is a mark placed on the neck.
rows.anchor: تعلط أقواما بميسم بارق ... وتقطم أوباشا زنيما ومسندا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Hudhalī poet threatens humiliating abuse through menstrual leather, caustic eye treatment, and foul nasal irrigation as another form of invective.
rows.anchor: متى ما أشأ غير زهو الملو ... ك أجعلك رهطا على حيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem's terms mean a leather garment worn during menstruation, a plant whose sap burns the eyes, kohl rubbed on stone, and reed water described as especially foul.
rows.anchor: والرهط: جلد تلبسه المرأة أيام الحيض. والصاب: شجر له لبن يحرق العين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling something by its opposite can express an omen or hopeful anticipation: a bitten person is called safe, the thirsty 'soon watered,' and a deadly desert a place of escape.
rows.anchor: ومن المقلوب: أن يوصف الشيء بضد صفته للتطير والتفاؤل، كقولهم للديغ: سليم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opposite naming can intensify description: the sun is called dark for its brilliance, and a crow one-eyed for its sharp sight.
rows.anchor: وللمبالغة في الوصف، كقولهم للشمس: جونة، لشدة ضوئها. وللغراب: أعور، لحدة بصره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opposite labels can be mockery, as when a black man is called father of the white and a white man father of the black.
rows.anchor: وللاستهزاء، كقولهم للحبشي: أبو البيضاء. وللأبيض: أبو الجون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb's people call him forbearing and prudent sarcastically, as one might call an idiot intelligent or a fool forbearing.
rows.anchor: قول قوم شعيب: إنك لأنت الحليم الرشيد [هود: 87]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet's address 'O forbearing one' is sarcastic, accusing the person of failing to act gently.
rows.anchor: يا حلي ... م إنك لم تأس أسوا رفيقا

words: لا تركضوا وارجعوا إلى ما أترفتم فيه
rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah identifies God's call not to flee but to return to their luxuries as mockery of people running from punishment.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: ومن الاستهزاء قول الله تعالى: فلما أحسوا بأسنا إذا هم منها يركضون (12) لا تركضوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras mocks defeated Kindah by asking where they are going, meaning they should turn back.
rows.anchor: هلا سألت جموع كن ... دة يوم ولوا: أين أينا؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret the taunt as reversing the words to mean the addressee is actually base and humiliated.
rows.anchor: فبعض الناس يذهب به هذا المذهب، أي أنت الذليل المهان.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as 'noble in your own eyes': Abū Jahl had boasted that no one between Mecca's hills was more powerful or honored.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم يريد: أنت العزيز الكريم عند نفسك. وهو معنى تفسير ابن عباس لأن أبا جهل قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣarīm names both night and dawn; here it means black as night, since night and day each break away from the other.
rows.anchor: قال الله سبحانه: فأصبحت كالصريم (20) [القلم: 20] ، أي سوداء كالليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sadfah can mean either darkness or light because each veils the other as it arrives.
rows.anchor: وللظلمة: سدفة. وللضوء: سدفة. وأصل السدفة: السترة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣārikh can mean either the person crying for help or the helper who cries in response.
rows.anchor: وللمستغيث: صارخ. وللمغيث: صارخ، لأن المستغيث يصرخ في استغاثته،

words: وإن ظنا أن يقيما حدود الله
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓann can mean certainty because it contains an element of certainty; Ibn Qutayba reads each cited occurrence in that sense.
rows.anchor: ولليقين: ظن، لأن في الظن طرفا من اليقين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A common construction omits a possessive head noun, promotes its dependent noun into its place, and assigns the verb to that dependent.
rows.anchor: من ذلك: أن تحذف المضاف وتقيم المضاف إليه مقامه وتجعل الفعل له.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ask the town means ask its people: the omitted possessive head is inhabitants.
rows.anchor: وسئل القرية التي كنا فيها [يوسف: 82] أي سل أهلها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The calf was made to drink into their hearts means that love of the calf was put into their hearts.
rows.anchor: وأشربوا في قلوبهم العجل [البقرة: 93] أي حبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hajj is known months means the time for Hajj falls in known months.
rows.anchor: والحج أشهر معلومات [البقرة: 197] أي وقت الحج.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled measure in life and death means a doubled punishment in life and a doubled punishment after death.
rows.anchor: إذا لأذقناك ضعف الحياة وضعف الممات-[الإسراء: 75] أي ضعف عذاب الحياة وضعف عذاب الممات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer itself cannot be demolished; the omitted noun is houses or buildings of prayer.
rows.anchor: وقوله سبحانه: لهدمت صوامع وبيع وصلوات ومساجد [الحج: 40] فالصلوات لا تهدم، وإنما أراد بيوت الصلوات.

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes assign monasteries to Ṣābians, churches to Christians, prayer houses to Jews, and mosques to Muslims.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: الصوامع للصابئين، والبيع للنصارى، والصلوات: كنائس اليهود، والمساجد للمسلمين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town that expelled you means the inhabitants of the town expelled you.
rows.anchor: من قريتك التي أخرجتك [محمد: 13] أي أخرجك أهلها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day plotted means you plotted during the night and the day.
rows.anchor: بل مكر الليل والنهار [سبأ: 33] أي مكركم في الليل والنهار.

words: أجعلتم سقاية الحاج وعمارة المسجد الحرام كمن آمن بالله
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading supplies the person responsible for watering pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque: did you make that person equal to a believer?
rows.anchor: أجعلتم صاحب سقاية الحاج وعمارة المسجد الحرام، كمن آمن؟!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the question compares the acts of watering pilgrims and maintaining the sanctuary with faith in God and striving in His path.
rows.anchor: ويكون يريد: أجعلتم سقاية الحاج كإيمان من آمن بالله وجهاده؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'piety is the one who believes' likewise uses piety for the person who possesses it.
rows.anchor: ولكن البر من آمن بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Hudhalī line says a wine shop walks among the people, using the shop for its owner.
rows.anchor: يمشي بيننا حانوت خمر ... من الخرس الصراصرة القطاط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Dhuʾayb's wine poem assigns the merchant's actions to the wine itself: the omitted referent is the wine seller.
rows.anchor: اللفظ للخمر والمعنى للخمار، أي يتوصل الخمار بالركب ليسير معهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Abū Dhuʾayb's next line, people bring a profit to the wine's owner, represented by the wine in the wording.
rows.anchor: أتوها بربح حاولته فأصبحت ... تكفت قد حلت وساغ شرابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kathīr describes palm groves by naming a Jewish man from Nata instead of the Jewish palms associated with him.
rows.anchor: حزيت لي بحزم فيدة تحدى ... كاليهودي من نطاة الرقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Let him call his council means let him call his people.
rows.anchor: فليدع ناديه (17) [العلق: 17] أي: أهله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He begins another ellipsis pattern: one verb is applied to two things though it belongs to only one, with a suitable verb understood for the other.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك أن توقع الفعل على شيئين وهو لأحدهما، وتضمر للآخر فعله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bāʾ can stand for min; Arabs say they drank bāʾ a particular water meaning they drank from it.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب: شربت بماء كذا وكذا، أي من ماء كذا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the two descriptions of the spring, bāʾ can mean from, or the verb can take the spring directly as its object.
rows.anchor: ويكون بمعنى يشربها عباد الله ويشرب منها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hudhalī poet's clouds drank from seawater; the line witnesses bāʾ meaning min.
rows.anchor: شربن بماء البحر ثم ترفعت ... متى لجج خضر لهن نئيج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAntarah's line about drinking from the water of al-Daḥraḍayn is another example of bāʾ meaning min.
rows.anchor: شربت بماء الدحرضين فأصبحت ... زوراء تنفر عن حياض الديلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'sent down with God's knowledge' uses bāʾ in the sense of from God's knowledge.
rows.anchor: فاعلموا أنما أنزل بعلم الله [هود: 14]

rows.speaker: بعض أهل السلف
rows.claim: A member of the early generations advised his son not to lie or use speech resembling lies, to keep him from sliding from habitual equivocation into falsehood.
rows.anchor: قال بعض أهل السلف لابنه: (يا بني لا تكذبن ولا تشبهن بالكذب)

words: وإنا أو إياكم لعلى هدى أو في ضلال مبين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ attributes the balanced alternative to indirect address: one of us is astray and one guided, while God knows the Messenger is guided and his opponents astray; it tactfully says one of us lies.
rows.anchor: فكذبته من وجه هو أحسن من التصريح، كذلك قال الفراء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect phrasing resembles telling someone who contradicts you that one of us must be lying, while intending him without bluntly naming him.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما تقول للرجل يكذبك ويخالفك: إن أحدنا لكاذب. وأنت تعنيه،

words: فإن كنت في شك مما أنزلنا إليك
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation addresses the Prophet but intends people who doubt, following an Arab convention of speaking to one person while meaning another.
rows.anchor: فإن كنت في شك مما أنزلنا إليك فسئل الذين يقرؤن الكتاب من قبلك [يونس: 94] ففيه تأويلان:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proverb 'I mean you, neighbor, so listen' exemplifies a speaker addressing one person while directing the message to someone else.
rows.anchor: إياك أعني واسمعي يا جارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to the Prophet gives counsel to believers; the following verse's plural 'what you do' supports a broader audience.
rows.anchor: الخطاب للنبي، صلى الله عليه وسلم، والمراد بالوصية والعظة المؤمنون، يدلك على ذلك أنه قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to ask those sent before him, meaning ask the communities reached by earlier messengers—here the People of the Book—while the intended audience is polytheists.
rows.anchor: وسئل من أرسلنا من قبلك من رسلنا أجعلنا من دون الرحمن آلهة يعبدون (45) [الزخرف: 45]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kumayt's praise poem for the Prophet is cited as an Arab example of this indirect mode of address.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذا قول الكميت في مدح رسول الله، صلى الله عليه وسلم :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet names the camel's load as ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib but means ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, substituting the father for the son.
rows.anchor: أراد: (عبد الله بن عباس) فذكر أباه مكانه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṣaltān intended to say Jarīr surpassed al-Farazdaq in poetry but used their grandfathers' names to fit the verse.
rows.anchor: أراد: «أرى جريرا بذ الفرزدق شعره» فلم يمكنه فذكر جده.

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbī identifies the person called al-Ḥārithiyyūn as Yazīd ibn Hubayr; the poet used the name under metrical pressure.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الكلبي: هو (يزيد بن هوبر) فاضطر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aws meant 'son of Ḥudhaym,' a pre-Islamic physician, but omitted son to satisfy the line.
rows.anchor: أراد: (ابن حذيم) وهو طبيب كان في الجاهلية:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Mayyādah meant two ibexes on each side, but his wording gives one ibex on each side under poetic constraint.
rows.anchor: أراد: وعلين من كل جانب، فلم يمكنه فقال: ووعل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Najm calls the camel's sire her maternal cousin, substituting one kinship term for another.
rows.anchor: أراد: فحلها: فجعله ابن خالها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet says Christians killed the Messiah but means the Jews.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : مثل النصارى قتلوا المسيح أراد: اليهود:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yalab is leather straps worn beneath helmets; the quoted line mistakes or treats them as iron.
rows.anchor: واليلب: سيور تجعل تحت البيض، فتوهمه حديدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruʾbah's phrase 'silver or sulfur gold' is listed as another inversion or substitution in poetic wording.
rows.anchor: وقال رؤبة : أو فضة أو ذهب كبريت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Najm reverses the relation in 'like lightning's gleam in its deceptive lightning' for 'the deceptive gleam of its lightning.'
rows.anchor: أراد: بخلب برقه، فقلب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet intended 'someone to rely on' but reversed the relation as 'someone upon whom to rely.'
rows.anchor: أراد: إن لم يجد يوما من يتكل عليه.

words: ومثل الذين كفروا كمثل الذي ينعق بما لا يسمع
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God neither errs nor is forced; the intended comparison is the disbelievers and the preacher addressing them, like a caller to something that cannot hear, with 'our likeness' omitted from the wording.
rows.anchor: والله تعالى لا يغلط ولا يضطر، وإنما أراد: ومثل الذين كفروا ومثلنا في وعظهم كمثل الناعق بما لا يسمع،

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ instead supplies 'the likeness of the one admonishing the disbelievers,' omitted as in 'ask the town' for its people.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : أراد: ومثل واعظ الذين كفروا، فحذف، كما قال: وسئل القرية التي كنا فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keys weighed down a band means their weight made the band bend under them.
rows.anchor: مفاتحه لتنوأ بالعصبة [القصص: 76]

words: لقد خلقنا الإنسان في أحسن تقويم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created the human being and proportioned his form with the finest adjustment.
rows.anchor: يريد: عدلنا خلقه، وقومناه أحسن تعديل وتقويم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lowly are the weak, chronically ill, children, and those unable to find a way or means; sāfil is formed like ʿāl from the verbs safala and ʿalā.
rows.anchor: والسافلون: هم الضعفاء والزمنى الأطفال، ومن لا يستطيع حيلة، ولا يجد سبيلا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse resembles the return to decrepit age: old people become confused and unsteady, weakened in body, sight, hearing, and ability to act righteously.
rows.anchor: ومنكم من يرد إلى أرذل العمر [النحل: 70]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who did good deeds while strong are not deprived of their reward in old age; God continues to credit it without cutting or reducing it.
rows.anchor: فإنهم في حال الكبر غير منقوصين، لأنا نعلم أنا لو لم نسلبهم القدرة والقوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Loss means deficiency; the believers who believe, do good, and counsel truth and patience are not diminished.
rows.anchor: والخسر: النقصان إلا الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet reports that God tells the recording angels to continue writing a servant's healthy deeds during illness until God takes him.
rows.anchor: إذا مرض عبدي فاكتبوا له ما كان يعمل في صحته، حتى أعاقبه أو أقبضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question means: what makes a person deny God's repayment according to deeds, when God is the wisest of judges?
rows.anchor: فما يكذبك أيها الإنسان بالدين؟ أي: بمجازاتي إياك بعملك وأنا أحكم الحاكمين؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These expressions exaggerate by describing an event as though it nearly happened; readers understand the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: وينوون في جميعه يكاد يفعل، وكلهم يعلم المراد به.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anonymous poet says a valley hyena eats a man's neighbor and trees throw him, though trees cannot throw anyone, as deliberate exaggeration.
rows.anchor: تركوا جارهم يأكله ... ضبع الوادي ويرميه الشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A seasonal poem personifies Suhayl as urinating in date wine because its rising coincides with the drink spoiling as dates ripen.
rows.anchor: وهذا وقت يذهب فيه الفضيخ، لأنه يكون من البسر، والبسر يصير عند طلوع هذه الأنجم رطبا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dukayn personifies night as carrying off the sun's soul; night has removed the sun as death removes a living being's soul.
rows.anchor: فجعل الشمس روحا عرج بها الليل. والأصل في هذا كله: أن كل حيوان يموت تقبض روحه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rummah says camels drink from one star and then another, but means their riders navigate by successive stars.
rows.anchor: يقول: تهتدي بكوكب طلع أول الليل، حتى إذا غاب اهتدت بكوكب آخر طالع في السحر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muzarrid imagines spiders growing gray and old in an elderly man's hair to express how long they have nested there; the image borrows from unmarried women who grow old at home.
rows.anchor: وإنما أراد طول مكث العناكب في رأسه، فجعلهن قد شبن وعنسن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Musayyib ibn ʿAlas says trees were summoned for help, using trees for a huge crowd; Arabs likewise say someone came with thorn and trees of a great army.
rows.anchor: أراد أنه دعا عليهم الخلق يستنصرهم، فضرب الشجر مثلا لكثرة الناس والعوام تقول: جاءنا بالشوك والشجر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muttaʾaka means food: Arabs say they reclined at someone's place to mean that they ate there.
rows.anchor: وأعتدت لهن متكأ [يوسف: 31] أي طعاما، يقال: اتكأنا عند فلان، أي طعمنا.
